statement: Students who are taught to memorize facts are poorly prepared for the problems they will face as adults.
Universities should require every student to complete a substantial period of community service before graduating.
Honest criticism, even when it is unwelcome, is far more useful to a person's development than praise.

Some people believe that college students should choose their courses primarily according to their intellectual interests. Others believe that students should choose courses primarily according to their usefulness in a future career.
Many of the most important discoveries in science have resulted from accident rather than from careful planning.

Claim: Universities should reward excellent teaching as highly as they reward excellent research. Reason: Most students benefit more directly from good instruction than from the research their professors publish.
The more people rely on technology to perform everyday tasks, the less capable they become of solving problems on their own.
Governments should fund scientific research only when it promises clear practical applications for the public that pays for it.
In most professions, being a broadly knowledgeable generalist is more valuable than being a highly trained specialist.

Some people believe that scientists are responsible for how the results of their research are eventually used. Others believe that scientists' responsibility ends with the pursuit of accurate knowledge.
Success in any demanding field, whether in the arts, the sciences, or business, depends more on persistence than on natural talent.

Claim: Communities gain more from small, locally owned businesses than from large national chains. Reason: Local business owners have a personal stake in the long-term well-being of the places where they operate.
The character of a great city is created by its ordinary residents rather than by its planners and architects.
Large cities should prohibit private automobiles from their central business districts and rely instead on public transportation, cycling, and walking.
Long-term planning is largely futile, because circumstances change too quickly for detailed plans to remain useful.

Some people believe that historic buildings should be preserved even at considerable cost. Others believe that communities should replace old structures whenever new construction would better serve current needs.
Decisions based on systematic analysis of data are almost always better than decisions based on experience and intuition.
Claim: Children should begin studying a second language in their earliest years of school. Reason: Young children acquire new languages more easily than adolescents or adults do.
The value of a work of art cannot be measured by how many people admire it.
Schools should replace traditional letter grades with detailed written evaluations of each student's strengths, weaknesses, and progress.
People generally learn more from their failures than from their successes, because failure forces them to reexamine their assumptions.
Some people believe that leaders should consult widely before making important decisions. Others believe that effective leaders must be willing to act decisively without waiting for consensus.
No translation can fully capture the meaning of a great work of literature, so readers should study important works in their original languages.
Claim: Fame is an unreliable measure of a person's accomplishments. Reason: Public attention is often driven more by novelty and visibility than by the quality of a person's work.
Effective leaders rarely change their minds once they have announced a decision, because frequent reversals undermine the confidence of their followers.
Public museums should offer free admission to all visitors, even if doing so requires reducing their collections or programs.
As a field of study becomes more established and its methods more standardized, it inevitably becomes less creative.
Some people believe that the arts should receive substantial public funding. Others believe that artists and arts organizations should depend on audiences and private supporters for their survival.
When solving difficult problems, groups working together generally produce better ideas than talented individuals working alone.
Claim: The results of publicly funded research should be freely available to everyone. Reason: Knowledge produced with public money belongs to the public that paid for it.
The most significant advances in a field usually come from people who were trained outside of it.
Organizations should fill leadership positions by promoting current employees rather than by hiring from outside.
The architecture of a city reveals more about the values of its people than its official documents do.
Some people believe that schools should emphasize teaching young people to cooperate. Others believe that schools should emphasize teaching young people to compete.
Humor is an undervalued tool for examining serious subjects, often revealing truths that solemn discussion tends to obscure.
Claim: Governments should protect wilderness areas even when those areas have no apparent economic use. Reason: The value of unspoiled nature cannot be fully expressed in economic terms.
A society that places too much value on tradition will find it difficult to make meaningful progress.
Parents should limit the amount of time their children spend in organized competitive activities such as sports leagues and academic contests.
The popular entertainment of a period tells us more about a society than its formal institutions do.
Some people believe that learning online can be just as effective as learning in a classroom. Others believe that face-to-face instruction offers benefits that no technology can replace.
The easy availability of information through digital devices has made people less knowledgeable rather than more.
Claim: All students, not only those planning technical careers, should study advanced mathematics. Reason: Mathematical study develops habits of rigorous reasoning that are useful in every field.
A person's true character is revealed more clearly by small daily choices than by dramatic decisions made in moments of crisis.
Public libraries should devote most of their budgets to digital resources rather than to printed books.
Most people would be happier and more productive if they owned fewer possessions and spent more of their resources on experiences.
Some people believe that complex public decisions are best left to experts. Others believe that ordinary citizens should have a direct role in making such decisions.
Truly original ideas are extremely rare; nearly all innovation consists of combining existing ideas in new ways.
Claim: The best way to understand a culture is to examine the objects its people use in everyday life. Reason: Ordinary objects reflect values and habits that people seldom state openly.
